## Part 1 · Why two languages?

**Python** (Guido van Rossum, 1991) was designed as a general-purpose language that reads like pseudocode. When DNA sequencing started producing *text* at scale (2005–2010), Python's string handling and its "glue" nature made it the language of pipelines: reads, files, tools, web services.

**R** (Ross Ihaka & Robert Gentleman, University of Auckland, 1993) is the open-source descendant of **S** (John Chambers, Bell Labs, 1976), a language *built for statistics*. In 2001 **Bioconductor** was founded on R, and since then most statistical methods for genomics (limma, edgeR, **DESeq2**) have been published as R packages first.

| | Python | R |
|---|---|---|
| Born | 1991, general purpose | 1993, statistics (from S, 1976) |
| Natural unit | string, list, dict | vector, data frame |
| Genomics home | Biopython, pysam, scanpy, PyTorch | Bioconductor: DESeq2, edgeR, Seurat |
| Plots | matplotlib (a library) | `plot()` is built into the language |
| Where you meet it | pipelines, machine learning, web | statistics, figures for the paper |

**Neither is "the real one".** A typical genomics project runs a Python (or shell) pipeline to produce a table of counts, then an R notebook to test hypotheses and draw the figures.

## Part 2 · Same idea, two syntaxes

The first thing to learn is that the differences are mostly *surface*. Here is the same tiny program.

::: {.two-col}
::: {}
<span class="lang-tag py">Python</span>
```{.pyodide}
gene = "COMT"          # a variable holding text
n = 271                # a number
print(gene, "has", n, "amino acids")

for base in "ATG":     # a loop over letters
    print(base)

def gc_content(dna):   # a function
    g = dna.count("G")
    c = dna.count("C")
    return (g + c) / len(dna)

print(gc_content("ATGCCGGAGG"))
```
:::
::: {}
<span class="lang-tag r">R</span>
```{.webr}
gene <- "COMT"         # a variable holding text
n <- 271               # a number
cat(gene, "has", n, "amino acids\n")

for (base in c("A", "T", "G")) {   # a loop over letters
  cat(base, "\n")
}

gc_content <- function(dna) {      # a function
  bases <- strsplit(dna, "")[[1]]
  mean(bases %in% c("G", "C"))
}

gc_content("ATGCCGGAGG")
```
:::
:::

### The four differences that actually matter

1. **Indexing starts at 0 in Python and at 1 in R.** `dna[0]` in Python is the first letter; `substr(dna, 1, 1)` in R is the first letter. Half of all coordinate bugs in genomics come from this. (BED files are 0-based; GTF/VCF files are 1-based.)
2. **Python works on one string; R works on vectors.** In R, almost everything is a vector, so `mean(bases %in% c("G","C"))` computes GC content without a loop. Python needs a loop or `str.count`.
3. **Assignment**: `=` in Python, `<-` in R (R also accepts `=`).
4. **Blocks**: Python uses indentation; R uses `{ }`.

::: {.yourturn}
In the cells above, change the sequence to `"ATGAAATTT"` and predict the GC content **before** you run.
:::

## Part 3 · Biology as strings

The coding sequence of **COMT** (catechol-*O*-methyltransferase, chromosome 22) is 816 letters. We will read it from a FASTA file, then do what every sequence tool does: count, reverse-complement, translate.

::: {.two-col}
::: {}
<span class="lang-tag py">Python</span>
```{.pyodide}
def read_fasta(path):
    seq = []
    for line in open(path):
        if not line.startswith(">"):
            seq.append(line.strip())
    return "".join(seq)

cds = read_fasta("data/COMT_cds.fa")
print(len(cds), "nt")
print(cds[:30])
gc = (cds.count("G") + cds.count("C")) / len(cds)
print("GC content:", round(gc * 100, 1), "%")
```
:::
::: {}
<span class="lang-tag r">R</span>
```{.webr}
read_fasta <- function(path) {
  lines <- readLines(path)
  paste(lines[!startsWith(lines, ">")], collapse = "")
}

cds <- read_fasta("data/COMT_cds.fa")
cat(nchar(cds), "nt\n")
cat(substr(cds, 1, 30), "\n")
bases <- strsplit(cds, "")[[1]]
gc <- mean(bases %in% c("G", "C"))
cat("GC content:", round(gc * 100, 1), "%\n")
```
:::
:::

### Reverse complement

DNA is double-stranded; a read may come from either strand. The reverse complement is *reverse* the string, then *complement* each letter.

::: {.two-col}
::: {}
<span class="lang-tag py">Python</span>
```{.pyodide}
complement = {"A": "T", "T": "A", "G": "C", "C": "G"}
rc = "".join(complement[b] for b in reversed(cds))
print(rc[:20])
```
:::
::: {}
<span class="lang-tag r">R</span>
```{.webr}
complement <- c(A = "T", T = "A", G = "C", C = "G")
rc <- paste(rev(complement[bases]), collapse = "")
cat(substr(rc, 1, 20), "\n")
```
:::
:::

### The genetic code is a dictionary

64 codons → 21 outcomes (20 amino acids + stop). In Python this is a **dict**; in R it is a **named vector**. The string below lists the amino acids in the standard TCAG order.

::: {.two-col}
::: {}
<span class="lang-tag py">Python</span>
```{.pyodide}
bases = "TCAG"
aas = "FFLLSSSSYY**CC*WLLLLPPPPHHQQRRRRIIIMTTTTNNKKSSRRVVVVAAAADDEEGGGG"
codon_table = {}
i = 0
for a in bases:
    for b in bases:
        for c in bases:
            codon_table[a + b + c] = aas[i]
            i += 1

def translate(dna):
    protein = ""
    for i in range(0, len(dna) - 2, 3):
        protein += codon_table[dna[i:i+3]]
    return protein

protein = translate(cds)
print(protein[:30], "...", protein[-5:])
print(len(protein) - 1, "amino acids + stop")
```
:::
::: {}
<span class="lang-tag r">R</span>
```{.webr}
b <- c("T", "C", "A", "G")
aas <- strsplit("FFLLSSSSYY**CC*WLLLLPPPPHHQQRRRRIIIMTTTTNNKKSSRRVVVVAAAADDEEGGGG", "")[[1]]
codons <- character(0)
for (x in b) for (y in b) for (z in b) codons <- c(codons, paste0(x, y, z))
codon_table <- setNames(aas, codons)

translate <- function(dna) {
  n <- nchar(dna) %/% 3
  starts <- seq(1, by = 3, length.out = n)
  cod <- substring(dna, starts, starts + 2)
  paste(codon_table[cod], collapse = "")
}

protein <- translate(cds)
cat(substr(protein, 1, 30), "...", substr(protein, nchar(protein) - 4, nchar(protein)), "\n")
cat(nchar(protein) - 1, "amino acids + stop\n")
```
:::
:::

### One letter, one amino acid: rs4680 (Val158Met)

The most studied variant in COMT is **rs4680**: a G→A change in codon 158 that turns **valine (GTG)** into **methionine (ATG)** and reduces enzyme activity 3–4 fold. The reference genome carries the G. Watch the off-by-one:

::: {.two-col}
::: {}
<span class="lang-tag py">Python</span>
```{.pyodide}
i = (158 - 1) * 3              # codon 158 → 0-based offset 471
print("codon 158:", cds[i:i+3], "=", codon_table[cds[i:i+3]])
mutant = cds[:i] + "A" + cds[i+1:]
print("mutant   :", mutant[i:i+3], "=", translate(mutant)[157])
```
:::
::: {}
<span class="lang-tag r">R</span>
```{.webr}
i <- (158 - 1) * 3 + 1         # codon 158 → 1-based position 472
cat("codon 158:", substr(cds, i, i + 2), "=", codon_table[substr(cds, i, i + 2)], "\n")
mutant <- cds
substr(mutant, i, i) <- "A"
cat("mutant   :", substr(mutant, i, i + 2), "=", substr(translate(mutant), 158, 158), "\n")
```
:::
:::

::: {.trap}
Python `cds[471:474]` and R `substr(cds, 472, 474)` are **the same three letters**. If you copy a 1-based coordinate from a VCF or GTF file into Python without subtracting 1, you translate the wrong codon and never notice.
:::

## Part 4 · Biology as tables

Once reads are counted, everything is a **table**: one row per gene, one column per sample or attribute. Python's table object is the pandas **DataFrame**; R's is the built-in **data.frame**. The five verbs you need: *read, filter, sort, group, summarize*.

`chr22_genes.tsv` lists all 1,747 GENCODE genes on chromosome 22.

::: {.two-col}
::: {}
<span class="lang-tag py">Python</span>
```{.pyodide}
import pandas as pd
genes = pd.read_csv("data/chr22_genes.tsv", sep="\t")
print(genes.shape)
print(genes["gene_type"].value_counts().head(5))

pc = genes[genes["gene_type"] == "protein_coding"]      # filter
print(len(pc), "protein-coding genes")
print(pc["length_bp"].median(), "bp median length")

longest = genes.sort_values("length_bp", ascending=False) # sort
print(longest[["gene_name", "length_bp"]].head(3))

# group + summarize
print(genes.groupby("gene_type")["length_bp"].median().sort_values(ascending=False).head(4))
```
:::
::: {}
<span class="lang-tag r">R</span>
```{.webr}
genes <- read.delim("data/chr22_genes.tsv")
dim(genes)
head(sort(table(genes$gene_type), decreasing = TRUE), 5)

pc <- genes[genes$gene_type == "protein_coding", ]       # filter
cat(nrow(pc), "protein-coding genes\n")
cat(median(pc$length_bp), "bp median length\n")

longest <- genes[order(-genes$length_bp), ]              # sort
head(longest[, c("gene_name", "length_bp")], 3)

# group + summarize
head(sort(tapply(genes$length_bp, genes$gene_type, median), decreasing = TRUE), 4)
```
:::
:::

### Joining two tables

`chr22_expression.tsv` is the output of an RSEM run on 100,000 real RNA-seq reads (BIOL419 Lab 4). Joining it to the gene table lets us ask: *which kinds of genes are expressed?*

::: {.two-col}
::: {}
<span class="lang-tag py">Python</span>
```{.pyodide}
expr = pd.read_csv("data/chr22_expression.tsv", sep="\t")
print(expr.sort_values("TPM", ascending=False)[["gene_name", "gene_type", "TPM"]].head(3))

m = genes.merge(expr[["gene_id", "TPM"]], on="gene_id")
frac_on = m.groupby("gene_type")["TPM"].apply(lambda s: (s > 1).mean())
print(frac_on.sort_values(ascending=False).head(4))
print(expr[expr["gene_name"] == "COMT"])
```
:::
::: {}
<span class="lang-tag r">R</span>
```{.webr}
expr <- read.delim("data/chr22_expression.tsv")
head(expr[order(-expr$TPM), c("gene_name", "gene_type", "TPM")], 3)

m <- merge(genes, expr[, c("gene_id", "TPM")], by = "gene_id")
frac_on <- tapply(m$TPM > 1, m$gene_type, mean)
head(sort(frac_on, decreasing = TRUE), 4)
expr[expr$gene_name == "COMT", ]
```
:::
:::

::: {.yourturn}
The top-expressed genes are immunoglobulin genes (*IGLC2*, *IGLV2-23*). What kind of cell was sequenced? (This is the L9 idea — same genome, different program — now answered from a table.)
:::

## Part 5 · Plots and a first statistical test

R's `plot()`, `hist()`, `boxplot()` are part of the language. In Python you import matplotlib. We follow the *publication-figure* rules from the CADSA workshop: set the **canvas size in inches first**, shrink margins, and add axes and labels yourself.

::: {.two-col}
::: {}
<span class="lang-tag py">Python</span>
```{.pyodide}
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
import numpy as np
fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(3.2, 3.2))
ax.hist(np.log10(genes["length_bp"]), bins=30, color="grey")
ax.set_xlabel("log10 gene length (bp)")
ax.set_ylabel("Number of genes")
for side in ["top", "right"]:
    ax.spines[side].set_visible(False)
plt.tight_layout()
plt.show()
```
:::
::: {}
<span class="lang-tag r">R</span>
```{.webr}
#| fig-width: 3.2
#| fig-height: 3.2
par(mar = c(4, 4, 1, 1))
hist(log10(genes$length_bp), breaks = 30, col = "grey80",
     main = "", xlab = "", ylab = "", axes = FALSE)
axis(1, line = 0.1); axis(2, line = 0.1)
title(xlab = "log10 gene length (bp)", line = 2)
title(ylab = "Number of genes", line = 2)
```
:::
:::

### A t-test on real RNA-seq counts

The **airway** dataset (Himes et al. 2014): airway smooth-muscle cells from 4 donors, each untreated and treated with the steroid dexamethasone → 8 samples. Is gene *ENSG00000152583* (SPARCL1) changed by treatment?

::: {.two-col}
::: {}
<span class="lang-tag py">Python</span>
```{.pyodide}
from scipy import stats
cts = pd.read_csv("data/airway_counts.tsv", sep="\t", index_col=0)
meta = pd.read_csv("data/airway_metadata.tsv", sep="\t")
logc = np.log2(cts + 1)
ctrl = meta["id"][meta["dex"] == "control"]
trt  = meta["id"][meta["dex"] == "treated"]
g = "ENSG00000152583"
print(logc.loc[g].round(2))
print(stats.ttest_ind(logc.loc[g, trt], logc.loc[g, ctrl]))
```
:::
::: {}
<span class="lang-tag r">R</span>
```{.webr}
cts  <- read.delim("data/airway_counts.tsv", row.names = 1)
meta <- read.delim("data/airway_metadata.tsv")
logc <- log2(cts + 1)
ctrl <- meta$id[meta$dex == "control"]
trt  <- meta$id[meta$dex == "treated"]
g <- "ENSG00000152583"
round(unlist(logc[g, ]), 2)
t.test(unlist(logc[g, trt]), unlist(logc[g, ctrl]))
```
:::
:::

Notice how R prints the whole test (confidence interval, means) in one line of code — this is what "statistics is first-class" means. Notice also that this test is **wrong for 19,271 genes at once** and ignores that the four donors are paired; Lecture 11 fixes both.

## Part 6 · Reads: the text sequencing produces

A FASTQ record is four lines: name, sequence, `+`, quality. Each quality character encodes a Phred score: `Q = ord(char) − 33`, and the probability the base is wrong is 10^(−Q/10). `reads_5k.fastq` has 5,000 real 100-nt reads from ENCODE.

::: {.two-col}
::: {}
<span class="lang-tag py">Python</span>
```{.pyodide}
reads = []
with open("data/reads_5k.fastq") as f:
    while True:
        name = f.readline()
        if not name:
            break
        seq = f.readline().strip()
        f.readline()                      # the '+' line
        qual = f.readline().strip()
        reads.append((seq, qual))

print(len(reads), "reads of", len(reads[0][0]), "nt")
q = [ord(c) - 33 for c in reads[0][1]]
print("first read qualities:", q[:10])
# mean quality per position
L = len(reads[0][0])
mean_q = [sum(ord(r[1][i]) - 33 for r in reads) / len(reads) for i in range(L)]
print([round(x, 1) for x in mean_q[::10]])
```
:::
::: {}
<span class="lang-tag r">R</span>
```{.webr}
lines <- readLines("data/reads_5k.fastq")
seqs  <- lines[seq(2, length(lines), by = 4)]
quals <- lines[seq(4, length(lines), by = 4)]
cat(length(seqs), "reads of", nchar(seqs[1]), "nt\n")
q <- utf8ToInt(quals[1]) - 33
cat("first read qualities:", q[1:10], "\n")
# mean quality per position: a 5000 x 100 matrix
Q <- t(sapply(quals, function(s) utf8ToInt(s) - 33))
round(colMeans(Q)[seq(1, 100, by = 10)], 1)
```
:::
:::

The Python version loops read-by-read; the R version builds a 5,000 × 100 **matrix** and takes column means. Same answer, two ways of thinking — and this is exactly why R feels natural once data are rectangular.

## Part 7 · Working like a scientist

- **Ecosystems.** Python packages come from PyPI (`pip install`) or conda; R packages from CRAN (`install.packages`) and **Bioconductor** (`BiocManager::install("DESeq2")`). A tool published in a paper is usually on one of these.
- **Notebooks are lab notebooks.** Jupyter (`.ipynb`) and Quarto/R Markdown (`.qmd`, `.Rmd`) keep code, output and your comments together. This website is a Quarto document.
- **Reproducibility.** Record versions (`pip freeze`, `sessionInfo()`), set random seeds, never edit raw data by hand, keep the script that made every figure.
- **ChatGPT writes code; you verify it.** Use TRACE prompting, then run the code on a case you already know the answer to — *COMT codon 158 must be GTG; the protein must start with M* — before you trust it on new data.

### The five bugs that bit real papers

1. **0-based vs 1-based** coordinates (BED vs GTF/VCF).
2. **Strand**: a k-mer from the minus strand never matches unless you reverse-complement.
3. **Reference build**: GRCh37 positions pasted into a GRCh38 file (rs4680 is chr22:19,963,748 in GRCh38 but 19,951,271 in GRCh37).
4. **Excel turns gene names into dates**: *SEPT7* → "7-Sep", *MARCH1* → "1-Mar". About one fifth of published supplementary gene lists contain this error (Ziemann et al. 2016), which is why HGNC renamed these genes in 2020 (*SEPTIN7*, *MARCHF1*).
5. **Silent type coercion**: a column read as text because one row says "NA"; a p-value column sorted as strings ("1e-10" after "0.5").

## Part 8 · The mental model

> **Question → data shape → language → verify.**

| The data are… | Think… | Reach for… |
|---|---|---|
| Sequences, reads, files, a tool to glue | text | Python (or the shell) |
| One row per gene and columns of numbers | table | either; R if statistics come next |
| Counts with replicates, a hypothesis | table + uncertainty | R (DESeq2, edgeR, limma) |
| Images, deep learning, single cell at scale | arrays | Python (PyTorch, scanpy) |

**Wednesday's lab** does all of this on the same files, in both languages, and ends with you catching a bug in code that ChatGPT wrote.
